To qualify, the student must be **16 or older**, enrolled in a post-secondary program to improve occupational skills, and have paid tuition exceeding **$100** [2][3]. The tuition must be paid to a **Canadian institution (reported via T2202 form) or an eligible foreign institution (via TL11A)** [2][4].  

The **student must first use the credit** to offset their own tax liability before transferring any **unused amount to one parent** [2][3][4]. Parents claim the transferred amount on **line 32400** of their tax return [4]. Unused amounts beyond the $5,000 limit can be carried forward by the student [3][4].  

Note that **third-party payments (e.g., by parents)** are considered gifts to the student; if no qualifying expenses were paid, no credits can be claimed [5]. Certain additional expenses, like laptops, may qualify if deemed necessary for enrollment [4].  

For clarity: **Parents cannot directly claim a child’s tuition**—the student must initiate the transfer [4]. Provincial rules (e.g., Ontario’s matching $5,000 limit) may apply [4].

Eligibility requires the student to be **16 or older**, enrolled in skill-building programs, and to have paid tuition exceeding **$100** [3].  

The student must first use the credit to reduce their own tax payable before transferring any unused portion to a parent [3][4]. The transfer requires proper documentation, such as the **T2202** form for Canadian institutions or **TL11A** for international schools [2][3]. Parents can claim the transferred credit on line **32400** of their tax return, but only if the student completes the transfer section of their tax certificate [4].  

Note that **employer reimbursements** disqualify claims, and unused credits can be carried forward by the student [4]. While parents cannot directly claim a child’s tuition, they may benefit if the student opts to transfer the credit [4]. Always verify rules with tax advisors, as improper transfers may trigger penalties [1][3].
